text:
Robust Correlation Methods

The Problem with Outliers
Standard Pearson correlation is sensitive to outliers. A single extreme value can dramatically affect results:

# Create data with an outlier
set.seed(42)
x <- rnorm(50)
y <- 0.6 * x + rnorm(50, sd = 0.5)

# Add an outlier
x_outlier <- c(x, 4)
y_outlier <- c(y, -3)

# Compare correlations
r_clean <- cor(x, y)
r_outlier <- cor(x_outlier, y_outlier)

# Visualize
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(x, y, pch = 19, main = sprintf("Clean Data\nr = %.3f", r_clean))
abline(lm(y ~ x), col = "blue", lwd = 2)

plot(x_outlier, y_outlier, pch = 19,
     main = sprintf("With Outlier\nr = %.3f", r_outlier))
points(4, -3, col = "red", pch = 19, cex = 2)
abline(lm(y_outlier ~ x_outlier), col = "blue", lwd = 2)










Available Robust Methods
The plscmd package provides several robust correlation methods:



Method
Function
Description




Winsorized
winsorized_cor()
Trims extreme values


Biweight
biweight_midcor()
Downweights outliers


Percentage Bend
percentage_bend_cor()
Robust to outliers


Wrapper
robust_cor()
Unified interface





Winsorized Correlation
Winsorization replaces extreme values with less extreme ones:

# Winsorized correlation (default: trim 10% from each tail)
r_wins <- winsorized_cor(x_outlier, y_outlier, trim = 0.1)

cat("Pearson correlation:", round(r_outlier, 3), "\n")

Pearson correlation: 0.388 

cat("Winsorized correlation:", round(r_wins, 3), "\n")

Winsorized correlation: 0.725 

cat("True correlation (clean):", round(r_clean, 3), "\n")

True correlation (clean): 0.791 




Biweight Midcorrelation
Uses a weighting function that downweights outliers:

# Biweight midcorrelation
r_biweight <- biweight_midcor(x_outlier, y_outlier)

cat("Biweight midcorrelation:", round(r_biweight, 3), "\n")

Biweight midcorrelation: 0.681 




Percentage Bend Correlation
A robust method based on the percentage bend:

# Percentage bend correlation
r_pbend <- percentage_bend_cor(x_outlier, y_outlier, beta = 0.2)

cat("Percentage bend correlation:", round(r_pbend, 3), "\n")

Percentage bend correlation: 0.721 




Unified Interface
Use robust_cor() for a consistent interface:

# Compare all methods
methods <- c("pearson", "winsorized", "biweight", "percentage_bend")

results <- sapply(methods, function(m) {
  robust_cor(x_outlier, y_outlier, method = m)
})

comparison <- data.frame(
  Method = methods,
  Correlation = round(results, 3)
)

knitr::kable(comparison, caption = "Correlation Method Comparison")

Matrix Correlations
All robust methods work with matrices:

# For within-matrix correlations
set.seed(42)
X <- matrix(rnorm(100), nrow = 20, ncol = 5)

# Add some outliers
X[1, 1] <- 10
X[1, 2] <- -8

# Compute correlation matrices
cor_pearson <- cor(X)
cor_robust <- robust_cor(X, method = "biweight")

cat("Pearson X1-X2 correlation:", round(cor_pearson[1, 2], 3), "\n")

Pearson X1-X2 correlation: -0.606 

cat("Biweight X1-X2 correlation:", round(cor_robust[1, 2], 3), "\n")

Biweight X1-X2 correlation: 0.443 

# For cross-matrix correlations, use individual pairs
x1 <- X[, 1]
y1 <- rnorm(20)
y1[1] <- 10  # Add outlier

cat("\nCross-matrix correlations:\n")


Cross-matrix correlations:

cat("Pearson:", round(cor(x1, y1), 3), "\n")

cat("Biweight:", round(robust_cor(x1, y1, method = "biweight"), 3), "\n")

Biweight: 0.165

text:
Understanding Package Internals

The PLS Algorithm
The core PLS computation involves these steps:

# Pseudocode for PLS
# 1. Compute cross-covariance matrix
R <- t(X) %*% Y  # or correlation matrix

# 2. Singular Value Decomposition
svd_result <- svd(R)

# 3. Extract components
u <- svd_result$u  # Brain saliences
v <- svd_result$v  # Behavior saliences
s <- svd_result$d  # Singular values

# 4. Compute scores
usc <- X %*% u     # Brain scores
vsc <- Y %*% v     # Behavior scores



Key Internal Functions
Explore the internal functions to understand the computation:

# rri_xcor: Compute cross-correlation/covariance matrix
?rri_xcor

No documentation for 'rri_xcor' in specified packages and libraries:
you could try '??rri_xcor'

# Example usage
X <- matrix(rnorm(50), nrow = 10, ncol = 5)
Y <- matrix(rnorm(30), nrow = 10, ncol = 3)

# Correlation mode
R_cor <- rri_xcor(X, Y, cormode = 0)
cat("Correlation matrix dimensions:", dim(R_cor), "\n")

Correlation matrix dimensions: 5 3 

# Covariance mode
R_cov <- rri_xcor(X, Y, cormode = 2)
cat("Covariance matrix dimensions:", dim(R_cov), "\n")

Covariance matrix dimensions: 5 3 




Bootstrap Resampling
Understanding how bootstrap samples are created:

# rri_boot_order: Generate bootstrap sample indices
# Arguments: num_subj_lst (subjects per group), num_cond, num_boot
n_subj <- 10
n_cond <- 3
num_boot <- 5

# Generate bootstrap sample orders
boot_result <- rri_boot_order(num_subj_lst = c(n_subj), num_cond = n_cond,
                               num_boot = num_boot)
boot_orders <- boot_result$boot_order
cat("Generated", boot_result$new_num_boot, "bootstrap samples\n")

Generated 5 bootstrap samples

cat("Each sample has", n_subj * n_cond, "indices\n")

Each sample has 30 indices

cat("First bootstrap order:", head(boot_orders[, 1], 15), "...\n")

First bootstrap order: 1 6 7 5 9 2 10 3 1 4 11 16 17 15 19 ...




Permutation Testing
How permutation orders are generated:

# rri_perm_order: Generate permutation orders
# Arguments: num_subj_lst, num_cond, num_perm
num_perm <- 5
perm_orders <- rri_perm_order(num_subj_lst = c(n_subj), num_cond = n_cond,
                               num_perm = num_perm)
cat("Generated", num_perm, "permutation orders\n")

Generated 5 permutation orders

cat("First permutation:", head(perm_orders[, 1], 15), "...\n")

text:
Building Custom Workflows

Custom Analysis Pipeline
Here’s a complete workflow for a research project:

# Step 1: Load and prepare data
prepare_pls_data <- function(brain_file, behav_file, groups) {
  # This would load your actual data
  # For demo, we simulate
  n_subj <- 25
  n_regions <- 50
  n_behav <- 4
  n_cond <- 2

  brain <- matrix(rnorm(n_subj * n_cond * n_regions),
                   nrow = n_subj * n_cond, ncol = n_regions)
  behav <- matrix(rnorm(n_subj * n_behav), nrow = n_subj, ncol = n_behav)

  list(brain = brain, behav = behav, n_subj = n_subj, n_cond = n_cond)
}

# Step 2: Quality control
quality_control <- function(data) {
  # Check for missing data
  report <- pls_check_missing(list(data$brain), verbose = FALSE)

  # Check for outliers (simple z-score method)
  z_scores <- scale(data$brain)
  n_outliers <- sum(abs(z_scores) > 3, na.rm = TRUE)

  list(
    missing_pct = report$overall_pct * 100,  # Convert to percentage
    n_outliers = n_outliers,
    passed = report$overall_pct < 0.20 && n_outliers < 0.01 * length(data$brain)
  )
}

# Step 3: Run analysis with options
run_pls_pipeline <- function(data, n_perm = 1000, n_boot = 1000) {
  # Stack behavioral data
  stacked_behav <- do.call(rbind,
                            replicate(data$n_cond, data$behav, simplify = FALSE))

  # Run analysis
  result <- pls_analysis(
    datamat_lst = list(data$brain),
    num_subj_lst = c(data$n_subj),
    num_cond = data$n_cond,
    option = list(
      method = 3,
      num_perm = n_perm,
      num_boot = n_boot,
      stacked_behavdata = stacked_behav,
      impute_method = "mean",
      verbose = FALSE
    )
  )

  result
}

# Step 4: Generate report
generate_report <- function(result, output_dir = "results") {
  if (!dir.exists(output_dir)) dir.create(output_dir)

  # Summary table
  summary <- pls_summary_table(result)
  write.csv(summary, file.path(output_dir, "summary_table.csv"))

  # Significant LVs
  sig_lvs <- which(result$perm_result$sprob < 0.05)

  if (length(sig_lvs) > 0) {
    cat("Significant LVs found:", paste(sig_lvs, collapse = ", "), "\n")

    # Save results for each significant LV
    for (lv in sig_lvs) {
      # Brain saliences
      brain_df <- data.frame(
        Region = 1:nrow(result$u),
        Salience = result$u[, lv],
        BSR = result$boot_result$compare_u[, lv],
        SE = result$boot_result$u_se[, lv]
      )
      write.csv(brain_df,
                file.path(output_dir, sprintf("LV%d_brain_saliences.csv", lv)))
    }
  }

  cat("Report saved to:", output_dir, "\n")
}

# Execute the pipeline
data <- prepare_pls_data("brain.csv", "behav.csv", groups = 1)
qc <- quality_control(data)
cat("QC passed:", qc$passed, "\n")

QC passed: TRUE 

if (qc$passed) {
  result <- run_pls_pipeline(data, n_perm = 500, n_boot = 500)
  generate_report(result)
}

Significant LVs found: 1 
Report saved to: results 




Batch Processing Multiple Datasets

# Process multiple datasets
datasets <- list(
  study1 = list(brain = brain1, behav = behav1),
  study2 = list(brain = brain2, behav = behav2),
  study3 = list(brain = brain3, behav = behav3)
)

results <- lapply(names(datasets), function(name) {
  cat("Processing:", name, "\n")

  data <- datasets[[name]]
  stacked_behav <- do.call(rbind, replicate(n_cond, data$behav, simplify = FALSE))

  result <- pls_analysis(
    datamat_lst = list(data$brain),
    num_subj_lst = c(nrow(data$behav)),
    num_cond = n_cond,
    option = list(
      method = 3,
      num_perm = 1000,
      num_boot = 1000,
      stacked_behavdata = stacked_behav,
      verbose = FALSE
    )
  )

  # Save individual results
  saveRDS(result, sprintf("%s_pls_result.rds", name))

  result
})

names(results) <- names(datasets)

Real-World Example: Multi-Group Analysis

# Simulate a two-group study (e.g., patients vs controls)
set.seed(42)

n_controls <- 20
n_patients <- 18
n_regions <- 40
n_behav <- 3
n_cond <- 2

# Control group data
brain_controls <- matrix(rnorm(n_controls * n_cond * n_regions),
                          nrow = n_controls * n_cond, ncol = n_regions)

# Patient group data (with altered brain-behavior relationship)
brain_patients <- matrix(rnorm(n_patients * n_cond * n_regions),
                          nrow = n_patients * n_cond, ncol = n_regions)

# Behavioral data
behav_controls <- matrix(rnorm(n_controls * n_behav), nrow = n_controls, ncol = n_behav)
behav_patients <- matrix(rnorm(n_patients * n_behav), nrow = n_patients, ncol = n_behav)

# Add signal (different patterns for each group)
stacked_behav_controls <- do.call(rbind, replicate(n_cond, behav_controls, simplify = FALSE))
stacked_behav_patients <- do.call(rbind, replicate(n_cond, behav_patients, simplify = FALSE))

# Controls: regions 1-10 positively correlate with behavior 1
for (r in 1:10) {
  brain_controls[, r] <- brain_controls[, r] + 0.5 * stacked_behav_controls[, 1]
}

# Patients: weaker relationship
for (r in 1:10) {
  brain_patients[, r] <- brain_patients[, r] + 0.2 * stacked_behav_patients[, 1]
}

# Stack data for multi-group analysis
datamat_lst <- list(brain_controls, brain_patients)
stacked_behavdata <- rbind(stacked_behav_controls, stacked_behav_patients)

# Run multi-group PLS
result_multigroup <- pls_analysis(
  datamat_lst = datamat_lst,
  num_subj_lst = c(n_controls, n_patients),
  num_cond = n_cond,
  option = list(
    method = 3,
    num_perm = 500,
    num_boot = 500,
    stacked_behavdata = stacked_behavdata,
    verbose = FALSE

)

library(ggplot2)

set.seed(42)

# Create simulated data with clear signal
n_subj <- 40
n_regions <- 40
n_behav <- 5
n_cond <- 1  # Single condition for clearer visualization

# Behavioral data
behavdata <- matrix(rnorm(n_subj * n_behav), nrow = n_subj, ncol = n_behav)
colnames(behavdata) <- c("Working_Memory", "Attention", "Processing_Speed",
                          "Verbal_Fluency", "Executive_Function")

# Brain data with injected signal
brain_data <- matrix(rnorm(n_subj * n_regions),
                      nrow = n_subj, ncol = n_regions)

# Inject strong signal in some regions
for (r in 1:8) {
  brain_data[, r] <- brain_data[, r] + 0.7 * behavdata[, 1]
}
for (r in 9:14) {
  brain_data[, r] <- brain_data[, r] - 0.5 * behavdata[, 2]
}

# Create region names (simulating brain regions)
region_names <- c(
  paste0("L_", c("DLPFC", "VLPFC", "ACC", "Insula", "Hippocampus",
                  "Amygdala", "Thalamus", "Caudate")),
  paste0("R_", c("DLPFC", "VLPFC", "ACC", "Insula", "Hippocampus",
                  "Amygdala", "Thalamus", "Caudate")),
  paste0("L_", c("V1", "V2", "MT", "FFA", "PPA", "IPS", "SPL", "IPL",
                  "STS", "TPJ", "Precuneus", "PCC")),
  paste0("R_", c("V1", "V2", "MT", "FFA", "PPA", "IPS", "SPL", "IPL",
                  "STS", "TPJ", "Precuneus", "PCC"))
)

# Run PLS
result <- pls_analysis(
  datamat_lst = list(brain_data),
  num_subj_lst = c(n_subj),
  num_cond = n_cond,
  option = list(
    method = 3,
    num_perm = 500,
    num_boot = 500,
    stacked_behavdata = behavdata,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
)

cat("Analysis complete. LV1 p-value:", result$perm_result$sprob[1], "\n")

Combined Summary Figure
The plot_lv_summary() function creates a multi-panel figure:

                        behav_names = colnames(behavdata),

                               behav_names = colnames(behavdata),

text:
What is PLS?
Partial Least Squares (PLS) is a multivariate statistical technique that finds linear combinations of variables from two data matrices that have maximum covariance with each other.

When to Use PLS
PLS is ideal when you have:

Two sets of variables you want to relate (e.g., brain measures and behaviors)
More variables than observations (common in neuroimaging)
Multicollinearity in your predictors
A desire to find patterns rather than predict specific outcomes



PLS vs. Other Methods



Method
Use Case




PLS
Find patterns relating two variable sets


PCA
Reduce dimensionality of one variable set


CCA
Find correlations between two sets (requires n > p)


Regression
Predict one outcome from predictors

Data Structure
The plscmd package expects data in a specific format:

Brain Data (datamat_lst)
A list of matrices, where each matrix represents a group:

Rows = subjects
Columns = brain variables (voxels, ROIs, connections)

n_regions <- 50
n_groups <- 2
n_conditions <- 3  # e.g., rest, task1, task2

# Create data for each group
# Each group's data is stacked: (n_subjects * n_conditions) x n_regions
group1_data <- matrix(rnorm(n_subj_per_group * n_conditions * n_regions),
                       nrow = n_subj_per_group * n_conditions,
                       ncol = n_regions)
group2_data <- matrix(rnorm(n_subj_per_group * n_conditions * n_regions),
                       nrow = n_subj_per_group * n_conditions,
                       ncol = n_regions)

# Put into a list
datamat_lst <- list(group1_data, group2_data)

# Check dimensions

cat("Group 2 dimensions:", dim(datamat_lst[[2]]), "\n")

ImportantData Stacking Convention



Within each group matrix, data is stacked by condition within subject:

Rows 1 to n_conditions: Subject 1’s data across conditions

And so on…





Behavioral Data (behavdata or stacked_behavdata)
A matrix of behavioral measures:

Rows = subjects (matching the brain data)
Columns = behavioral variables

Setup

# Source the plscmd package (all files)
source("setup.R")

set.seed(42)

# Create simulated data with a known signal
n_subj <- 30
n_regions <- 50
n_behav <- 4
n_cond <- 1  # Single condition for clearer demonstration
n_groups <- 1

# Create behavioral data
behavdata <- matrix(rnorm(n_subj * n_behav), nrow = n_subj, ncol = n_behav)
colnames(behavdata) <- c("Memory", "Attention", "Speed", "Accuracy")

# Create brain data with some regions correlated with behavior
brain_data <- matrix(rnorm(n_subj * n_regions),
                      nrow = n_subj, ncol = n_regions)

# Inject signal: regions 1-10 correlate with Memory (behavior 1)
for (r in 1:10) {
  brain_data[, r] <- brain_data[, r] + 0.5 * behavdata[, 1]
}

# Regions 11-15 correlate with Attention (behavior 2)
for (r in 11:15) {
  brain_data[, r] <- brain_data[, r] + 0.4 * behavdata[, 2]
}

# Run PLS analysis
result <- pls_analysis(
  datamat_lst = list(brain_data),
  num_subj_lst = c(n_subj),
  num_cond = n_cond,
  option = list(

    num_perm = 1000,
    num_boot = 1000,
    stacked_behavdata = behavdata,

)

title: Lesson 2: Understanding PLS Results
text:
Permutation Testing

Why Permutation Tests?
PLS always finds latent variables - even with random data. We need to test whether the observed patterns are statistically significant or could have occurred by chance.
Permutation testing:

Shuffles the correspondence between brain and behavior data
Runs PLS on the shuffled data
Repeats many times to build a null distribution
Compares observed singular values to null distribution



Interpreting Permutation Results

# Access permutation results
perm <- result$perm_result

# P-values for each LV
cat("Permutation p-values:\n")

Permutation p-values:

for (i in seq_along(perm$sprob)) {
  sig <- ifelse(perm$sprob[i] < 0.05, "*", "")
  cat(sprintf("  LV%d: p = %.4f %s\n", i, perm$sprob[i], sig))
}

  LV1: p = 0.0000 *
  LV2: p = 0.2358 
  LV3: p = 0.5315 
  LV4: p = 0.9980 




Visualizing the Null Distribution

library(ggplot2)

# Note: The permutation function stores counts, not individual values.
# Here we simulate what the null distribution would look like for illustration.
# In practice, the p-value tells us where the observed value falls.

observed_s <- result$s[1]
p_value <- perm$sprob[1]

# Simulate approximate null distribution based on observed data characteristics
set.seed(42)
null_mean <- observed_s * 0.5  # Null is typically centered lower
null_sd <- observed_s * 0.15
simulated_null <- rnorm(500, mean = null_mean, sd = null_sd)

df <- data.frame(s = simulated_null)

ggplot(df, aes(x = s)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed_s, color = "red", linewidth = 1.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = observed_s, y = Inf, label = sprintf("Observed\ns = %.2f", observed_s),
           vjust = 2, hjust = -0.1, color = "red", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(
    title = "LV1: Conceptual Null Distribution",
    subtitle = sprintf("Actual p = %.4f (from permutation test)", p_value),
    x = "Singular Value",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)














TipHow Many Permutations?




Minimum: 500 for exploratory analysis
Publication: 1,000 - 5,000
High precision: 10,000+

More permutations = more precise p-values, especially for small p-values.

title: Lesson 2: Understanding PLS Results
text:
Bootstrap Ratios

What Are Bootstrap Ratios?
While permutation tests tell us if an LV is significant, bootstrap ratios tell us which specific variables contribute reliably to that LV.
Bootstrap ratio = salience / standard error
This is analogous to a z-score:

|BSR| > 1.96 ≈ p < 0.05
|BSR| > 2.58 ≈ p < 0.01
|BSR| > 3.29 ≈ p < 0.001



Examining Bootstrap Ratios

boot <- result$boot_result

# Bootstrap ratios for brain saliences (LV1)
bsr_brain <- boot$compare_u[, 1]

# Standard errors
se_brain <- boot$u_se[, 1]

# Create a summary
bsr_summary <- data.frame(
  Region = 1:n_regions,
  Salience = result$u[, 1],
  SE = se_brain,
  BSR = bsr_brain,
  Significant = abs(bsr_brain) > 1.96
)

# Show regions with highest absolute BSR
top_regions <- bsr_summary[order(abs(bsr_summary$BSR), decreasing = TRUE), ]
head(top_regions, 10)


  





Visualizing Bootstrap Ratios

# Create region names
region_names <- paste0("Region_", 1:n_regions)

# Use the package's plotting function
p <- plot_bootstrap_ratios(result, lv = 1,
                            region_names = region_names,
                            show_all = TRUE)
print(p)














ImportantConservative Significance



The plscmd package uses a conservative criterion: a region is considered significant only if the lower bound of its confidence interval (|BSR| - SE) exceeds the threshold. This is more stringent than simply checking if |BSR| > threshold.

Behavioral Correlations

Understanding Behavior Results
For each LV, we can examine how behaviors correlate with the brain pattern:

# Original correlations (from bootstrap)
orig_corr <- boot$orig_corr[, 1]

# Confidence intervals
ll_corr <- boot$llcorr[, 1]  # Lower limit
ul_corr <- boot$ulcorr[, 1]  # Upper limit

# Create summary
behav_summary <- data.frame(
  Behavior = colnames(behavdata),
  Correlation = round(orig_corr, 3),
  CI_Lower = round(ll_corr, 3),
  CI_Upper = round(ul_corr, 3),
  Significant = sign(ll_corr) == sign(ul_corr)  # CI doesn't cross zero
)

print(behav_summary)

Attention Attention      -0.025        0        0        TRUE
Speed         Speed       0.417        0        0        TRUE

p <- plot_lv_correlations(result, lv = 1, behav_names = behav_names)

text:
Interpreting Results

A Complete Interpretation Workflow

# Step 1: Which LVs are significant?
cat("Step 1: Significant Latent Variables\n")

Step 1: Significant Latent Variables

cat("=====================================\n")

=====================================

sig_lvs <- which(perm$sprob < 0.05)
if (length(sig_lvs) > 0) {
  cat("Significant LVs:", paste(sig_lvs, collapse = ", "), "\n\n")
} else {
  cat("No significant LVs found.\n\n")
}

Significant LVs: 1 

# Step 2: For each significant LV, examine the pattern
for (lv in sig_lvs) {
  cat(sprintf("\nLV%d Analysis (p = %.4f)\n", lv, perm$sprob[lv]))
  cat(paste(rep("-", 40), collapse = ""), "\n")

  # Variance explained
  var_exp <- (result$s[lv]^2) / sum(result$s^2) * 100
  cat(sprintf("Variance explained: %.1f%%\n\n", var_exp))

  # Significant behaviors
  orig_corr <- boot$orig_corr[, lv]
  ll <- boot$llcorr[, lv]
  ul <- boot$ulcorr[, lv]
  sig_behav <- sign(ll) == sign(ul)

  cat("Significant behavioral correlations:\n")
  for (b in which(sig_behav)) {
    cat(sprintf("  %s: r = %.2f [%.2f, %.2f]\n",
                colnames(behavdata)[b], orig_corr[b], ll[b], ul[b]))
  }

  # Count significant brain regions
  bsr <- boot$compare_u[, lv]
  se <- boot$u_se[, lv]
  sig_pos <- sum((bsr - se) > 1.96)
  sig_neg <- sum((bsr + se) < -1.96)

  cat(sprintf("\nSignificant brain regions:\n"))
  cat(sprintf("  Positive: %d regions\n", sig_pos))
  cat(sprintf("  Negative: %d regions\n", sig_neg))
}


LV1 Analysis (p = 0.0000)

Common Pitfalls






WarningAvoid These Mistakes




Ignoring non-significant LVs’ patterns: Even if LV1 is not significant, don’t interpret the brain-behavior pattern.
Over-interpreting single regions: A pattern is defined by the whole brain, not individual regions.
Forgetting about multiple comparisons: Consider FDR correction if testing many regions.
Confusing correlation with causation: PLS finds associations, not causal relationships.

The Missing Data Problem
Missing data is common in research:

Participants drop out

Questionnaires have unanswered items


Types of Missing Data








Type
Description
Implication




MCAR
Missing Completely At Random
Safe to impute or delete


MAR
Missing At Random (conditional on observed data)
Imputation is valid


MNAR
Missing Not At Random
Imputation may be biased









ImportantWhy Not Just Delete?



Complete case deletion (listwise deletion):

Reduces sample size and power

title: Lesson 4: Handling Missing Data
text:
Creating Data with Missing Values
Let’s create a realistic dataset with missing values:

# Create complete data first
n_subj <- 40
n_regions <- 30
n_behav <- 4
n_cond <- 2

# Behavioral data
behavdata_complete <- matrix(rnorm(n_subj * n_behav), nrow = n_subj, ncol = n_behav)
colnames(behavdata_complete) <- c("Memory", "Attention", "Speed", "Accuracy")

# Brain data
brain_complete <- matrix(rnorm(n_subj * n_cond * n_regions),
                          nrow = n_subj * n_cond, ncol = n_regions)

# Add signal
stacked_behav_complete <- do.call(rbind, replicate(n_cond, behavdata_complete, simplify = FALSE))
for (r in 1:8) {
  brain_complete[, r] <- brain_complete[, r] + 0.6 * stacked_behav_complete[, 1]
}

# Now introduce missing values
brain_missing <- brain_complete
behav_missing <- behavdata_complete

# 5% missing in brain data (scattered)
n_brain_missing <- round(0.05 * length(brain_missing))
brain_missing[sample(length(brain_missing), n_brain_missing)] <- NA

# 10% missing in one behavioral variable
behav_missing[sample(n_subj, round(0.10 * n_subj)), 2] <- NA

# 3% missing in another behavioral variable
behav_missing[sample(n_subj, round(0.03 * n_subj)), 4] <- NA

cat("Brain data missing:", sum(is.na(brain_missing)), "values\n")

Single Imputation

Mean Imputation
The simplest approach - replace missing values with the column mean:

# Impute with mean
imputed_mean <- pls_impute(
  datamat_lst = list(brain_missing),

Biases standard errors downward

Multiple Imputation

Why Multiple Imputation?
Single imputation treats imputed values as if they were known. Multiple imputation accounts for uncertainty:

Create multiple (m) complete datasets with different imputed values
Analyze each dataset separately
Pool results using Rubin’s rules



Creating Multiple Imputations

# Create 5 imputed datasets

  datamat_lst = list(brain_missing),
  behavdata = stacked_behav_missing,
  method = "mean",  # Use "rf" for random forest if available
  m = 5,            # 5 imputations
  verbose = TRUE
)

text:
Rubin’s Rules for Pooling

Theory
When pooling results from multiple imputations:
Point estimate (pooled coefficient): \[\bar{\theta} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \hat{\theta}_i\]
Within-imputation variance: \[\bar{W} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} W_i\]
Between-imputation variance: \[B = \frac{1}{m-1} \sum_{i=1}^{m} (\hat{\theta}_i - \bar{\theta})^2\]
Total variance: \[T = \bar{W} + \left(1 + \frac{1}{m}\right) B\]


Using pool_estimates()

# Simulate results from 5 imputations
set.seed(123)
m <- 5

# Simulated singular values from each imputation
estimates <- matrix(
  c(2.1, 2.3, 2.0, 2.2, 2.15,  # LV1
    1.5, 1.4, 1.6, 1.45, 1.55, # LV2
    0.8, 0.9, 0.85, 0.82, 0.88), # LV3
  nrow = m, ncol = 3, byrow = FALSE
)

# Simulated variances (squared SEs)
variances <- matrix(0.01, nrow = m, ncol = 3)

# Pool the estimates
pooled <- pool_estimates(estimates, variances)

cat("Pooled estimates:\n")

Pooled estimates:

print(round(pooled$pooled, 3))

[1] 1.467 1.533 1.483 1.490 1.527

cat("\nTotal variance:\n")


Total variance:

print(round(pooled$total_var, 4))

[1] 0.5744 0.6811 0.4644 0.6464 0.5482

cat("\nFraction of Missing Information (FMI):\n")


Fraction of Missing Information (FMI):

print(round(pooled$fmi, 3))

[1] 0.983 0.985 0.978 0.985 0.982
